group.title: Make, do, take and have
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To choose what to do after thinking.
examples: We need to {make a decision} by Friday.
wrong: She made a decision, so she still didn’t know what to do.

words.meaning: To do something wrong without meaning to.
examples: Everyone {makes a mistake} sometimes.
wrong: I made a mistake, so every answer was right.

words.meaning: To try hard to do something.
examples: He {made an effort} to be polite.
wrong: She made an effort by not trying at all.

words.meaning: To get better or move closer to a goal.
examples: You are {making progress} with your English.
wrong: He made progress, so he is further from his goal than ever.

words.meaning: To earn money.
examples: She {makes money} by selling cakes.
wrong: He made money by giving all his savings away.

words.meaning: To say officially that you are not happy about something.
examples: I want to {make a complaint} about the room.
wrong: She was so happy with the hotel that she made a complaint.

words.meaning: To check that something is true or done.
examples: {Make sure} you lock the door.
wrong: I made sure the door was locked, so I never checked it.

words.meaning: To start a friendship with new people.
examples: It’s easy to {make friends} at summer camp.
wrong: He made friends by never talking to anyone.

words.meaning: To have an important effect, often a good one.
examples: A small gift can {make a difference}.
wrong: Her help made a difference, so nothing changed at all.

words.meaning: To give a reason, often not true, for not doing something.
examples: He always {makes an excuse} to miss practice.
wrong: She made an excuse and happily did the job.

words.meaning: To arrange a time to see a doctor or other person.
examples: I’d like to {make an appointment} with the dentist.
wrong: I made an appointment, so there’s no time arranged.

words.meaning: To move things so there is space for someone or something.
examples: Please {make room} for one more person.
wrong: We made room on the shelf by filling every space.

words.meaning: To earn the money you need to live.
examples: He {makes a living} as a taxi driver.
wrong: She makes a living from a hobby that pays nothing.

words.meaning: To say you will certainly do something.
examples: I {made a promise} to call her every day.
wrong: He made a promise, so he had no plan to do it.

words.meaning: To try as hard as you can.
examples: Just {do your best} in the exam.
wrong: She did her best by giving up after one minute.

words.meaning: To buy, sell or work with another company or person.
examples: We {do business} with firms in Asia.
wrong: They do business together, but they never trade or work together.

words.meaning: To harm or break something.
examples: The storm {did damage} to many houses.
wrong: The storm did damage, so every house was perfect.

words.meaning: To help someone in a kind way.
examples: Could you {do me a favor} and close the window?
wrong: He did me a favor by making my day harder.

words.meaning: To study a subject carefully to find new facts.
examples: She {does research} on ocean animals.
wrong: He did research by never reading or asking anything.

words.meaning: To be successful.
examples: He {did well} in his exams.
wrong: She did well and failed every test.

words.meaning: To stop working or doing something for a short rest.
examples: Let’s {take a break} and have a coffee.
wrong: We took a break by working all day without stopping.

words.meaning: To do something that could end badly.
examples: He {took a risk} and started his own company.
wrong: She took a risk by choosing the safest option.

words.meaning: To join in an activity or event.
examples: Twenty schools will {take part} in the contest.
wrong: He took part in the race by watching it from home.

words.meaning: To happen, especially at a planned time.
examples: The wedding will {take place} in June.
wrong: The meeting took place, so it never happened.

words.meaning: To look after someone or something.
examples: Can you {take care of} my cat this weekend?
wrong: She took care of the plants and never watered them.

words.meaning: To do something one after another.
examples: The children {take turns} on the swing.
wrong: They took turns, so everyone went at the same time.

words.meaning: To use a good chance or situation well.
examples: {Take advantage of} the sunny weather and go out.
wrong: He took advantage of the sale by paying full price.

words.meaning: To write down important things you hear or read.
examples: Students {take notes} during the lecture.
wrong: She took notes by just listening and writing nothing.

words.meaning: To sit down; often said politely.
examples: Please {take a seat}; the doctor is coming.
wrong: He took a seat and stood by the door all evening.

words.meaning: To accept that something is your job or your fault.
examples: You must {take responsibility} for your actions.
wrong: He took responsibility by blaming everyone else.

words.meaning: To start doing something to deal with a problem.
examples: We must {take action} to save the forest.
wrong: The city took action by doing nothing at all.

words.meaning: To do something slowly, without hurrying.
examples: There’s no rush; {take your time}.
wrong: She took her time and finished in a terrible hurry.

words.meaning: To try to do something, often for the first time.
examples: Can I {have a go} on your guitar?
wrong: He had a go at skiing without ever trying it.

words.meaning: To look at something quickly.
examples: Let me {have a look} at your homework.
wrong: I had a look at the photo with my eyes closed.

words.meaning: To relax or sleep for a short time.
examples: You look tired; go and {have a rest}.
wrong: She had a rest by running ten kilometers.

words.meaning: To talk with someone in a friendly, informal way.
examples: We {had a chat} over coffee.
wrong: We had a chat without saying a single word.

words.meaning: To disagree angrily with someone.
examples: They {had an argument} about money.
wrong: We had an argument because we agreed about everything.

words.meaning: To find it hard to do something.
examples: I {have trouble} sleeping when it’s hot.
wrong: He has trouble reading, so he reads very fast and easily.

words.meaning: To speak to someone briefly, often in private.
examples: Can I {have a word} with you after class?
wrong: He had a word with me but didn’t speak to me.

words.meaning: To not know something at all.
examples: I {have no idea} where my keys are.
wrong: I have no idea where he lives; it’s next door to me.
